$MRVL has lost about 50% of its value in one month. 

Today CEO Matt Murphy emailed every employee to explain it, under the subject line "Putting the Week in Perspective."

What happened, in his words:

1. Last week Marvell agreed to combine with $LITE. Murphy says "some of the initial analyst commentary and media coverage reflected a misunderstanding of the strategic rationale."

2. The large shareholders he met in Boston and New York "told a very different story." He says they understood the case for joining silicon and optics, and recognized Marvell's acquisition track record.

3. Their most common question was "why now?" His answer points to Inphi, which put Marvell ahead of the move to scale-out optics. Optics are now moving into scale-up and scale-in, and "customers are making important technology decisions now that will shape the next generation of AI infrastructure."

4. On the stock, he gives the number plainly. "Marvell shares declined approximately 51%, closely in line with the 49% average decline among our connectivity peers." $LITE saw a similar decline.

5. He ties that to a selloff across AI stocks. Part of the cause is "uncertainty about how long the current AI infrastructure investment cycle will continue." He adds that the midterms "brought increased attention" to data center expansion and "the possibility of additional restrictions."

6. His counterpoint is the longer window. "Marvell shares are still up approximately 66% year to date," ahead of both connectivity and broader AI peers, and he says the long-term trends behind AI infrastructure spending "remain strong."

7. He ends by telling staff the deal alone won't pay off. "Simply acquiring a company doesn't create value. It's what we do afterward." That part is still far off, because the deal isn't expected to close until the first half of 2028 and the two companies stay independent until then.

Intrator pointed to about $9B of customer prepayments and deposits expected over the next three months. An at-the-market program for up to 35M shares has been in place since September.

The Senate voted 73-25 Monday to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Trump has endorsed it, and more votes are expected this week.

The bill speeds up federal approvals for power plants and power lines, and it makes large data centers pay for the grid upgrades built to serve them, so those costs don’t land on regular electric customers.

I think the bill favors data centers that use behind the meter power generation, for two reasons.

On cost, Grid Strategies estimates data centers would pay about $55B in transmission charges over ten years under the bill, against roughly $20B at current rates.

On time, the median wait for a grid connection is already more than five years, per Berkeley Lab, while permitting a gas plant on site takes 6 to 18 months before construction starts.

Google’s $GOOG Wyoming campus shows what that looks like in practice. $AEP is building a 702 MW plant of Bloom Energy $BE fuel cells outside its regulated utility territory, and Google’s 20 year contract for the output pays for it, so no Wyoming household pays toward it.

$ARM

It’s been a while since I’ve taken a closer look at $ARM, but there have been some really interesting developments cooking in the background.

This week Google announced its new TPU 8i Max, the latest in its line of custom AI chips. Like TPU 8t and TPU 8i before it, it runs on Google’s own Arm-based Axion CPUs as the host, so Google’s newest AI chips are all being built around Arm, something the market seems to have overlooked.

Every TPU needs a CPU next to it to feed it data and run the work around it, which means every TPU Google adds pulls more Arm in with it.

Axion also runs Google’s regular cloud servers at up to 2x better price-performance than comparable x86 machines, and AI agent sandboxes run about 30% cheaper on it.

Arm-based servers were already more than 45% of server revenue in Q1, according to IDC, and Arm expects to pass 60% share across the top U.S. clouds by the end of 2026.

Google’s new TPUs are getting all the headlines, but don’t think for a second they’ll rise on their own. Every TPU ships with a CPU, and it’s built on Arm.

Great news for Arm.

Bullish ⚡️

I went through CoreWeave’s Q3 report and call line by line, and it’s the strongest neocloud print I’ve seen this year.

Revenue grew 168% to $3.66B, ahead of estimates, and adjusted operating income hit $379M against guidance of $200M to $260M.

Full-year guidance went up to $13.0B–$13.3B, and CoreWeave expects to exit 2026 at a $20B–$21B revenue run rate.

Demand is 10x available capacity through 2027, and every bit of 2028 capacity offered so far is already sold.

Backlog hit $132.5B, up 138% in a year. The part due within 24 months more than doubled to ~$48B.

Prices went up ~25% in July and another 10% after. Short-term capacity now sells for $40M+ per MW a year, and older Ampere and Hopper GPUs repriced 30–50% higher.

The interest bill everyone is worried about went from 25x operating income in Q1 to 2.2x in Q3. Over 75% of capex through 2027 is backed by investment-grade and enterprise customers, and management expects contracted cash flow to repay the debt.

130,000 GPUs come off contract in 2027 and 170,000 more in 2028. Re-signed at today’s prices, that’s close to $10B of run-rate revenue with zero new capex.

You simply are not bullish enough on AI compute.

RKLB $RKLB  我认为市场可能低估了 Rocket Lab 接下来的融资压力，未来的债务问题，可能比 Neutron （中子火箭）延期更值得关注。

昨天的财报其实相当不错。营收2.68亿美元，同比增长73%，在手订单35.7亿美元，季度经营现金流也终于转正。

但我反而开始担心另外一件事：RKLB 的业务规模增长很快，但它创造现金的能力，真的跟得上扩张速度吗？

它的FCF真的那么健康吗？

我认为这才是投资者在意的核心问题

2026年前9个月，RKLB 通过 ATM 增发融资39.12亿美元，同期经营现金净流出1.27亿美元，资本开支8420万美元。

公司现在账上有约47亿美元的现金和有价证券，看起来相当充裕。

但问题在于，这笔钱主要不是靠发射火箭赚来的，而是靠资本市场融资得来的。

我认为这两件事必须分开看。

再看 Iridium 的收购。

80亿美元的企业价值，其中涉及超过30亿美元的现金支出。RKLB 已经通过增发完成了收购所需的融资，甚至主动取消了原本36亿美元的过桥贷款。

但真正值得关注的，是它已经开始进入需要管理大规模债务的阶段。

Iridium 现有约17.75亿美元的贷款会在收购完成后继续保留。这意味着 RKLB 不仅要考虑自己的研发和扩产，还要面对合并后的利息、债务到期和资本分配问题。

与此同时，Neutron 首飞已经推迟到2027年。

即使首飞成功，后续的商业化、产能扩张和发射频率提升，依然需要持续投入。

一个典型问题出现了，RKLB是缺钱的。

过去 RKLB 可以依靠股价上涨，不断通过增发获得资金。但如果未来市场不愿意继续给出这么高的估值，它又该怎么融资？

继续增发，意味着稀释股东。

转向债务融资，意味着更多利息和杠杆。

尤其是当公司还想维持高速扩张的时候，我认为未来进一步利用债务融资的可能性并不低。

当然，Iridium 本身拥有稳定现金流，收购也可能改善 RKLB 的融资能力。所以我现在并不认为短期新增发债已经是必然事件。

我真正想表达的是，RKLB 可能正在从一个依靠估值融资的成长故事，逐渐进入需要证明资本回报的阶段。

过去市场愿意为它未来十年的增长付钱。

但接下来，市场可能越来越在意这些增长究竟需要投入多少钱，又能给股东留下多少现金。

这也是我最近研究 AI、半导体和数据中心公司时反复关注的问题。

当行业进入资本开支持续高企、增长逐渐需要更多资金支持的阶段，决定估值的就不只是收入增速了。
